=−q2m2​⟨[p,H]2⟩+q3m3​⟨[[p,H],p2]⟩\displaystyle=-\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}\langle[p,H]^{2}\rangle+\frac{q^{3}}{m^{3}}\langle[[p,H],p^{2}]\rangle
+q4m4​(⟨p4⟩−3​⟨p2⟩2)\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{q^{4}}{m^{4}}\Big(\langle p^{4}\rangle-3\langle p^{2}\rangle^{2}\Big) (60)
…\displaystyle\ldots

In the harmonic approximation, only the terms proportional to q2q^{2} are nonzero. As a result, only the first few expansion terms are needed as long as t≪1ω0t\ll\frac{1}{\omega_{0}} since f(n+1)/f(n)f^{(n+1)}/f^{(n)} is of order ω0\omega_{0}. Then one can solve for the saddle point tIt_{I} by solving f′​(tI)≈f′​(0)+f′′​(0)​tI=0f^{\prime}(t_{I})\approx f^{\prime}(0)+f^{\prime\prime}(0)t_{I}=0, which gives

i​tI=m2​(ω−q22​m)q2​σp2,it_{I}=\frac{m^{2}(\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m})}{q^{2}\sigma_{p}^{2}}, (61)

where

σp2≡⟨p2⟩−⟨p⟩2=⟨p2⟩.\displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{p}\equiv\langle p^{2}\rangle-\langle p\rangle^{2}=\langle p^{2}\rangle. (62)

In the last equality we use the fact that ⟨p⟩=0\langle p\rangle=0 for a V⁡(x)V(x) potential since ⟨p⟩∝⟨[x,H]⟩=0\langle p\rangle\propto\langle[x,H]\rangle=0. Although tIt_{I} is formally imaginary, its magnitude is small and close to the origin in the impulse regime. Since there is no pole around this saddle point, we can approximate the time integral by the saddle point and find

Stoy,d​(q,ω)\displaystyle S_{\text{toy},d}(q,\omega) ≈2​π−f′′​(tI)​ef⁡(tI)\displaystyle\approx\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{-f^{\prime\prime}(t_{I})}}\,e^{f(t_{I})}
=2​π​mq​σp​exp⁡(−m2​(ω−q22​m)22​q2​σp2).\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}m}{q\sigma_{p}}\exp\left(-\frac{m^{2}(\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m})^{2}}{2q^{2}\sigma_{p}^{2}}\right). (63)

For large energy depositions the Gaussian becomes narrowly peaked around ω=q2/2​m\omega=q^{2}/2m, and this reproduces the nuclear recoil limit [25].

In the presence of anharmonic interactions, other powers of qq will be present in the expansion of (60). In general, the f(n)f^{(n)} term will have a qnq^{n} term with coefficient of 𝒪⁡(λ).\mathcal{O}(\lambda). In this case, f(n+1)/f(n)∼q​ω0/mf^{(n+1)}/f^{(n)}\sim q\sqrt{\omega_{0}/m}. Higher orders will then be important in the expansion of f⁡(t)f(t) for sufficiently large qq or tt. For a given qq, the higher order corrections become relevant for |t|≳m/ω0/q∼1/ω​ω0|t|\gtrsim\sqrt{m/\omega_{0}}/q\sim 1/\sqrt{\omega\omega_{0}} in the impulse regime. Including these corrections is difficult in general, but we can continue to use the second order expansion giving (63) as long as |t|≲1/ω​ω0.|t|\lesssim 1/\sqrt{\omega\omega_{0}}. According to (61), this corresponds to a condition on how close ω\omega is to q2/(2​m)q^{2}/(2m). Since q2∼2​m​ωq^{2}\sim 2m\omega and σp2∼m​ω0,\sigma_{p}^{2}\sim m\omega_{0}, this implies that

|tI|∼|ω−q22​m|ω​ω0→|ω−q22​m|≲ω​ω0.|t_{I}|\sim\frac{|\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m}|}{\omega\omega_{0}}\rightarrow|\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m}|\lesssim\sqrt{\omega\omega_{0}}. (64)

We see that the distance of ω\omega from q22​m\frac{q^{2}}{2m} sets the size of tI,t_{I}, which in turn tells us the regime for the validity for the approximation (63). The condition (64) is approximately the same condition that ω\omega is within the Gaussian width in (63), and keeping terms in f⁡(t)f(t) only up to f′′​(0)f^{\prime\prime}(0) is self-consistent near ω=q22​m\omega=\frac{q^{2}}{2m}.

Therefore, in the presence of anharmonic interactions, the above structure factor result (63) remains valid in the impulse regime (52). The only modification is in σp2\sigma_{p}^{2}. Considering perturbations in V⁡(x)V(x) up to x4x^{4} and recalling that the expectation value is with respect to the full ground state, we find that

σp2=⟨p2⟩=m​ω02​(1−44​λ32+12​λ4+⋯)\sigma_{p}^{2}=\langle p^{2}\rangle=\frac{m\omega_{0}}{2}\Big(1-44\lambda_{3}^{2}+12\lambda_{4}+\cdots\Big) (65)

at leading order in λ3,λ4.\lambda_{3},\lambda_{4}. The nuclear recoil limit is again reproduced, with a small modification to the width of the Gaussian envelope due to anharmonic couplings. Note that in order to calculate the structure factor far from ω=q22​m,\omega=\frac{q^{2}}{2m}, we must include additional orders in f⁡(t)f(t) and tIt_{I}. We do not perform these higher order calculations for the final results in this paper since they have a negligible effect on the integrated rates, but we provide the procedure for completeness in App. C.

Finally, we approximate the effect that introducing the full crystal lattice has on this single atom result. Up until the evaluation of various moments of H′,H^{\prime}, the impulse approximation is fully model-independent. We just have to make an adjustment to the final evaluation of ⟨p2⟩\langle p^{2}\rangle. The states in the full crystal theory are smeared by the phonon density of states, so we calculate ⟨p2⟩\langle p^{2}\rangle via the following prescription

⟨p2⟩\displaystyle\langle p^{2}\rangle =m​ω02​(1+g​(λ))\displaystyle=\frac{m\omega_{0}}{2}\Big(1+g(\lambda)\Big)
→crystal∫d​ω′​D​(ω′)​m​ω′2​(1+g⁡(λ)),\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\mathrm{crystal}}\int d\omega^{\prime}D(\omega^{\prime})\frac{m\omega^{\prime}}{2}\Big(1+g(\lambda)\Big), (66)

where g⁡(λ)g(\lambda) is the anharmonic correction calculated in the single-atom potential. Essentially, we have used the average single phonon energy to calculate ⟨p2⟩.\langle p^{2}\rangle. In the harmonic limit, (63) then exactly matches the impulse result from [25].

In summary, in this section we have demonstrated the general behavior of anharmonic effects with qq and ω\omega. We have shown that they are indeed negligible at high qq and ω∼q2/2​md\omega\sim q^{2}/2m_{d}, consistent with the intuition that scattering can be described by elastic recoils of a free nucleus. The effects grow for q≪2​md​ω0q\ll\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}} and at low qq they may dominate the structure factor. This roughly matches onto the results of Refs. [37, 25], which found that for q<2​π/aq<2\pi/a anharmonic effects can have a large impact on the two-phonon rate .

IV Numerical results for 1D anharmonic oscillator

Having demonstrated the analytic behavior of the dynamic structure factor in the previous section, we now turn to obtaining numerical results using realistic potentials. We will perform concrete calculations for Si and Ge as representative materials while briefly commenting on others. As discussed in Sec. II.2, we adopt an empirical model of interatomic interactions that encodes the anharmonicity in the potential. We use this empirical model to calculate a single atom potential, which we then use to evaluate the structure factor numerically.

As stated in Sec. II.3, we start by fitting the single atom potential in a particular direction onto a 1D potential of the form,

Vd​(x)\displaystyle V_{d}(x) =12​md​ω02​x2+λ3​ω0​(2​md​ω0​x)3\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}m_{d}\omega_{0}^{2}x^{2}+\lambda_{3}\omega_{0}(\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}x)^{3}
+λ4​ω0​(2​md​ω0​x)4.\displaystyle\quad+\lambda_{4}\omega_{0}(\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}x)^{4}. (67)

In the fit, ω0,λ3,λ4\omega_{0},\lambda_{3},\lambda_{4} are free parameters but in order to reproduce the harmonic limit, we then make the replacement ω0=1/ω−1¯\omega_{0}=1/\overline{\omega^{-1}}, which is calculated from the phonon density of states and gives a slightly different numerical value. This is motivated by the harmonic case discussed in Sec. II.1. We do not consider anharmonic terms ∝xk\propto x^{k} for k≥5k\geq 5 as we observe that the anharmonic potential along any direction is dominated by the cubic and the quartic terms.

We find that the maximum anharmonicity is typically along the nearest neighbor direction (x,y,z)=(1,1,1)(x,y,z)=(1,1,1). For computing results, we will consider the potential along this direction, which represents maximum anharmonicity, as well as the potential in an orthogonal direction (x,y,z)=(1,−2,1)(x,y,z)=(1,-2,1), which represents an intermediate value for the anharmonicity. Using the aforementioned interatomic models, we find anharmonicity strengths ranging from λ3∼6×10−3\lambda_{3}\sim 6\times 10^{-3} to 10−210^{-2} and λ4∼(2−3)×10−4\lambda_{4}\sim(2-3)\times 10^{-4}. For Si and Ge, the results are same for either atom in the unit cell.

Given the 1D potential in (67), we find exact solutions of the 1D eigenvalue and eigenvector problem using a simple finite difference method. We take a first order discretization of the Laplace operator and solve the discretized time-independent Schrödinger equation in a box. The box grid interval size must be small enough to resolve the maximum momentum scales of interest, which in this case depends on the highest excited state needed in the calculation. Also, the minimum box size required depends on the spatial extent of the highest excited state used. As seen in Sec. III.3, the impulse approximation suffices for q>𝒪⁡(few)×2​md​ω0q>\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{few})\times\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}. Beyond this momentum, we no longer need to calculate excited states since the structure factor in the impulse limit is independent of the details of the highly excited states. The nth excited state is most relevant at momenta q∼n​2​m​ω0.q\sim\sqrt{n}\sqrt{2m\omega_{0}}. Therefore, to complete our calculation below the impulse limit, we include the first 10 excited states. The results for these eigenstates are converged above a box size of ∼10/2​m​ω0\sim 10/\sqrt{2m\omega_{0}} and grid size of ∼0.1/2​m​ω0\sim 0.1/\sqrt{2m\omega_{0}}.

We now use these numerical eigenstates and energies to calculate the structure factor in Eq. (27). We apply a prescription for the energy-conserving delta function similar to that used in the harmonic 1D oscillator, Eq. (15). The final result at momenta below the impulse regime (q<2​2​m​ω0q<2\sqrt{2m\omega_{0}}) is,

S⁡(qCLOSE,\displaystyle S(q, OPENω)=2​π​∑dnd​|fd|2​∑f|⟨Φf|ei​q​x|Φ0⟩|2\displaystyle\omega)=2\pi\sum_{d}n_{d}~|f_{d}|^{2}\sum_{f}\left|\matrixelement{\Phi_f}{e^{iqx}}{\Phi_0}\right|^{2}
×12​π​f​(n)​σ2​e−(ω−f⁡(n)​ω0)22​f​(n)​σ2×Θ⁡(ωmax−ω),\displaystyle\times\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi f(n)\sigma^{2}}}e^{-\frac{(\omega-f(n)\omega_{0})^{2}}{2f(n)\sigma^{2}}}\times\Theta(\omega_{\mathrm{max}}-\omega), (68)

where

ω0\displaystyle\omega_{0} =(∫d​ω​ω−1​D​(ω))−1,\displaystyle=\Big(\int d\omega\omega^{-1}D(\omega)\Big)^{-1}, (69)
σ\displaystyle\sigma =∫d​ω​ω​D​(ω)ω0−1ω02,\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{\int d\omega\omega D(\omega)}{\omega_{0}}-\frac{1}{\omega_{0}^{2}}}, (70)
ωmax\displaystyle\omega_{\mathrm{max}} =f⁡(n)×(min⁡(ω)|D⁡(ω)=0)\displaystyle=f(n)\times(\mathrm{min}(\omega)|D(\omega)=0) (71)

and f⁡(n),|Φ0⟩,|Φf⟩f(n),|\Phi_{0}\rangle,|\Phi_{f}\rangle are given by the numerically solved eigenenergies and eigenstates, respectively. D⁡(ω)D(\omega) is the single phonon density of states calculated with DFT [51]. In this work we assume equal couplings of DM with all nucleons so that fd=Adf_{d}=A_{d}, where AdA_{d} is the atomic mass number. In the equations above, we have included a sum over all atoms in the unit cell dd with density ndn_{d}, and in general the atomic potentials and density states can also depend on dd, although for Si and Ge we do not include this.

In the impulse regime (q>2​2​m​ω0q>2\sqrt{2m\omega_{0}}), we have shown in Sec. III.3 that the structure factor for any position-dependent potential is approximated by a Gaussian envelope,

S⁡(q,ω)≈∑dnd​|fd|2​2​πq2m2​⟨p2⟩​e−(ω−q22​m)22​q2m2​⟨p2⟩,S(q,\omega)\approx\sum_{d}n_{d}|f_{d}|^{2}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}\langle p^{2}\rangle}}e^{-\frac{\big(\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m}\big)^{2}}{2\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}\langle p^{2}\rangle}}, (72)

where the the expectation values are all computed in the ground state and adjusted to the average single phonon energy via (66). Now we simply use the numerical ground state of the anharmonic potential (67) to calculate ⟨p2⟩\langle p^{2}\rangle and therefore obtain the structure factor. Note that the anharmonic contribution is essentially negligible in the impulse limit, since corrections to ⟨p2⟩\langle p^{2}\rangle are ∝\propto λ32,λ4\lambda_{3}^{2},\lambda_{4}.

Fig. 7-8 shows numerical results on the structure factor for Si and Ge, taking the maximum anharmonicity in either case. In Fig. 7, the structure factor as a function of qq is shown. As ω\omega (and therefore minimum phonon number nn) is increased, there is a larger anharmonic correction at small qq. This can be understood by looking at the qq scalings discussed in Sec. III.2 and illustrated in Fig. 4 and Fig. 5. At low qq and thus DM mass, the contributions from the anharmonic structure factor can give smaller powers of q22​md​ω0\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}} compared to the leading harmonic term (q22​md​ω0)n\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{n}, so the enhancement grows with nn. At high qq, results converge to the harmonic result, consistent with our discussion of the impulse regime in Sec. III.3. We see this also in Fig. 8, which shows the structure factor at different qq. The impulse approximation becomes better as q≫2​md​ω0q\gg\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}, and is indistinguishable from the harmonic case.

IV.1 Impact on DM scattering rates

We now use the numerical results for the structure factor to compute the DM scattering rates for a range of DM masses and experimental thresholds. Our results are summarized in Figs. 9-10. We consider DM masses in the range ∼1−10\sim 1-10 MeV. The lower end of the mass range is chosen such that the momentum transfers are large enough to satisfy the condition for the incoherent approximation (i.e. q>2​π/aq>2\pi/a), while at the upper end of masses it is expected that scattering is described by the impulse approximation [25]. It is precisely this mass range where details of multiphonon production are important. We will also consider the two cases of scattering through heavy and light mediators. The goal will be to identify the region of parameter space where the anharmonic effects on the dynamic structure factor affect the scattering rates the most.

In the isotropic limit, the observed DM event rate per unit mass is given by [25]

R=14​π​ρT​ρχmχ​σpμχ2​∫d3​𝐯​f⁡(𝐯)v​∫q−q+d​q​∫ωthω+d​ω​q​|F~​(q)|2​S​(q,ω),R=\frac{1}{4\pi\rho_{T}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\sigma_{p}}{\mu_{\chi}^{2}}\int\!d^{3}{\bf v}\,\frac{f({\bf v})}{v}\int\displaylimits_{q_{-}}^{q_{+}}\!dq\,\int\displaylimits_{\omega_{\mathrm{th}}}^{\omega_{+}}\!d\omega\,q\,|\tilde{F}(q)|^{2}S(q,\omega), (73)

where ρχ\rho_{\chi} is the DM energy density, ρT\rho_{T} is the mass density of the target material, mχm_{\chi} is the DM mass, μχ\mu_{\chi} is the DM-nucleon reduced mass, σp\sigma_{p} is the DM-nucleon cross section, and f⁡(𝐯)f(\mathbf{v}) is the DM velocity distribution. The structure factor S⁡(q,ω)S(q,\omega) is given by our numerical results (68)-(72) and the integration bounds are determined by the kinematically allowed phase space

q±\displaystyle q_{\pm} ≡mχ​v​(1±1−2​ωthmχ​v2),\displaystyle\equiv m_{\chi}v\left(1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{2\omega_{\mathrm{th}}}{m_{\chi}v^{2}}}\right), (74)
ω+\displaystyle\omega_{+} ≡q​v−q22​mχ,\displaystyle\equiv qv-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\chi}}, (75)

where the energy threshold of the experiment is denoted by ωth\omega_{\mathrm{th}}. The qq-dependence of the DM-nucleus interaction can be encapsulated in the DM form factor F~​(q)\tilde{F}(q), where F~​(q)=1\tilde{F}(q)=1 indicates an interaction through a heavy mediator, and F~​(q)=q02/q2\tilde{F}(q)=q_{0}^{2}/q^{2} indicates an interaction through a light mediator for a reference momentum transfer of q0q_{0}.

Note that in general, the strength of the anharmonicity varies with the direction of the recoil of the nucleus, and the structure factor will depend on the direction of the momentum transfer. For simplicity, we are assuming that the anharmonicity strength is uniform in all directions. Our estimate with the maximum anharmonicity thus provides an upper bound on the anharmonic effects on DM scattering.

The DM mass sets the typical momentum-transfer scale qq of the scattering, and the experimental energy threshold ωth\omega_{\text{th}} sets the phonon number nn. Hence, to identify the DM masses and experimental thresholds where anharmonic effects start to become important, we first need to understand the qq-values where the anharmonic corrections are large for a particular phonon number nn. We can estimate this using the perturbation theory results in Sec. III.2. Note that in our numerical calculation, we find that λ3\lambda_{3} generally provides the larger anharmonic contribution, so we will focus on a purely cubic perturbation in this discussion.

For the analysis of a cubic perturbation discussed in Sec. III.2, we showed that anharmonic effects introduced additional terms to the nn-phonon structure factor of the form ∝\propto λ3ν⁡(n,i)​(q22​md​ω0)i\lambda_{3}^{\nu(n,i)}\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{i}, see (39). Therefore when qq is lower than the scale

q≲2​md​ω0​λ3ν​(n,i)/(2​(n−i)),q\lesssim\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\lambda_{3}^{\nu(n,i)/(2(n-i))}, (76)

terms in the anharmonic structure factor can be of comparable size to the harmonic structure factor. In order to find the largest qq-scale where the anharmonic contribution starts to become relevant, we can evaluate (76) for all positive i<ni<n, and find the minimum possible exponent of λ3\lambda_{3}. For n=2n=2 or 33, the minimum exponent is achieved for i=1i=1, for which ν⁡(n,1)=2\nu(n,1)=2. This gives a qq-scaling of q∼2​md​ω0​λ31/(n−i).q\sim\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\lambda_{3}^{1/(n-i)}. This tells us that for the 2-phonon case, the anharmonic contribution should begin to become important at q∼2​md​ω0​λ3,q\sim\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\lambda_{3}, while for the 3-phonon case, the anharmonic contribution becomes important at q∼2​md​ω0​λ31/2q\sim\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\lambda_{3}^{1/2}. For a larger number of phonons, this scaling is approximately q∼2​md​ω0​λ31/3q\sim\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\lambda_{3}^{1/3}. So we see that higher energy excitations have more significant anharmonic contributions at larger momentum transfers. Below the qq-scale identified above, the anharmonic contributions are expected to increase substantially with decreasing qq, as terms ∝q2​i\propto q^{2i} for i<ni<n dominate the harmonic scaling ∝q2​n\propto q^{2n}.

We now recast our analysis concretely in terms of DM mass and experimental energy thresholds as follows. For both massive and massless mediators, the event rate for n≥2n\geq 2 phonons is always dominated by the large qq portion of phase space and energy depositions near the threshold. Therefore the enhancement in the rate due to the anharmonicity roughly corresponds to the enhancement in structure factor evaluated at S⁡(q=2​mχ​v,ω=ωth)S(q=2m_{\chi}v,\omega=\omega_{\mathrm{th}}), where vv is the DM velocity. Inserting q=2​mχ​vq=2m_{\chi}v into the condition in (76) gives a condition on the DM mass:

mχ≲{2​md​ω0​λ32×10−3n=22​md​ω0​λ31/22×10−3n=32​md​ω0​λ31/32×10−3n>3,m_{\chi}\lesssim\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\lambda_{3}}{2\times 10^{-3}}&n=2\\ \frac{\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\lambda_{3}^{1/2}}{2\times 10^{-3}}&n=3\\ \frac{\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\lambda_{3}^{1/3}}{2\times 10^{-3}}&n>3,\end{cases} (77)

where 10−310^{-3} is the typical DM velocity. In order to determine the appropriate phonon number nn for a given ωth\omega_{\rm th} we must take into account the subtlety that each excitation energy is smeared across a width, as discussed in Sec. II.3 and also given in (70). To solve for the smallest nn that contributes appreciably above ωth\omega_{\rm th}, we solve the following equation:

ωth=n​ω0+n​σ,\omega_{\mathrm{th}}=n\omega_{0}+\sqrt{n}\sigma, (78)

where σ\sigma is the single-phonon width as defined in (70) and we have for simplicity taken f⁡(n)=n.f(n)=n.

Applying (77)-(78) to Si with ω0=31\omega_{0}=31 meV, σ=18\sigma=18 meV, and md=26m_{d}=26 GeV, we find the following results

mχ≲{0.2​MeV​λ310−2ωth=80​meV2.0​MeV​(λ310−2)1/2ωth=120​meV4.5​MeV​(λ310−2)1/3ωth≥160​meVm_{\chi}\lesssim\begin{cases}0.2\ \mathrm{MeV}\frac{\lambda_{3}}{10^{-2}}&\omega_{\mathrm{th}}=80\ \mathrm{meV}\\ 2.0\ \mathrm{MeV}\Big(\frac{\lambda_{3}}{10^{-2}}\Big)^{1/2}&\omega_{\mathrm{th}}=120\ \mathrm{meV}\\ 4.5\ \mathrm{MeV}\Big(\frac{\lambda_{3}}{10^{-2}}\Big)^{1/3}&\omega_{\mathrm{th}}\geq 160\ \mathrm{meV}\end{cases} (79)

Below these masses, anharmonic corrections become large. The last line applies for thresholds above 160 meV which corresponds to n≥4n\geq 4, and these nn-phonon terms all give the same condition on DM mass. Note that this is only a heuristic, which does not include for example the combinatorial pre-factors or cancellations in the perturbation theory calculation. Nonetheless, we do see the same qualitative features in the complete numerical result which is given in Fig. 9.

In order to generalize (79) to other materials, we give the necessary energy scales in Tab. 1. Despite large differences in ω0\omega_{0}, the momentum scale 2​md​ω0\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}} ends up being about the same in all crystals. Then the typical DM mass scale for anharmonic effects to become important is also about the same for a fixed phonon number nn. However, the differences in ω0\omega_{0} mean that the threshold corresponding to a given nn can vary significantly. For a given threshold, GaAs and Ge have the largest phonon number. Since anharmonic corrections become more important with larger nn, GaAs and Ge will therefore have larger anharmonic contributions compared to Diamond at the same threshold.

In Fig. 9, we present the ratio of scattering rates in the anharmonic case to the harmonic case in Si and Ge, taking two representative cases for the couplings. We also present the cross-sections corresponding to an observed rate of 3 events per kg-yr in Fig. 10. The bands depict the possible uncertainty that anharmonicity introduces to an experimental reach, with the solid line giving the harmonic result and the dot-dashed the result for maximal anharmonicity. We do not show the effects above the cross sections of σn≳10−28​cm2\sigma_{n}\gtrsim 10^{-28}~\text{cm}^{2} as for these large interaction strengths, the DM is expected to lose a significant energy in 1 km of Earth’s crust through scattering, thus rendering DM with such cross sections unobservable in underground direct detection experiments [52].

For mχ>10m_{\chi}>10 MeV, the typical qq becomes similar or larger than 2​md​ω0\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}, where there is negligible difference in the anharmonic and harmonic structure factors. The rates will also start to be dominated by the impulse regime q≫2​md​ω0q\gg\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}. In this case, the structure factor calculated with an anharmonic potential is nearly identical to that calculated in the harmonic case, as discussed in Sec. III.3. We have also seen this behavior with numerical computations in Fig. 8. The anharmonic and harmonic scattering rates are also essentially identical for DM masses mχ>10m_{\chi}>10 MeV.

For DM masses mχ<10m_{\chi}<10 MeV (i.e. q<2​md​ω0q<\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}), the ratio of the anharmonic to harmonic rate begins to grow with decreasing DM mass. As the typical qq decreases with decreasing DM mass, the leading anharmonic term ∝q22​md​ω0\propto\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}} grows faster compared to the harmonic term ∝(q22​md​ω0)n\propto\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{n} for n≥2n\geq 2. The effect is more pronounced for higher thresholds or equivalently higher nn, since the harmonic term is even more suppressed. Therefore at larger thresholds, the anharmonic effects start becoming important already at larger masses and also grows much more quickly as the DM mass is decreased. For a given DM mass, this also implies that the spectrum of events will have larger anharmonic corrections on the high energy tail of events. However, the rates are also highly suppressed in this tail, and only observable for high scattering cross sections.

At DM masses mχ<1m_{\chi}<1 MeV, the slope of the ratio of the anharmonic rate to the harmonic rate starts to decrease slightly, which is an artifact of the Brillouin zone momentum cutoff that we apply across all rate calculations. The incoherent and subsequent approximations are not guaranteed to be justified in this regime, so this effect should not be treated as physical. For sub-MeV DM masses, the phonons again should be treated as collective excitations, similar to the calculation of Ref. [37].

Lastly, we note an interesting feature that the anharmonic scattering rate is strictly greater than the harmonic rate in the entire parameter space that we probe. This is a consequence of the sign of the leading qq-scaling term q22​md​ω0\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}. For the production of an excited state |Φf⟩|\Phi_{f}\rangle in the crystal, the term in the dynamic structure factor ∝q2\propto q^{2} can only come from the term |⟨Φf|i​q​x|Φ0⟩|2|\langle\Phi_{f}|iqx|\Phi_{0}\rangle|^{2}, as the mixing term ∝⟨Φf|I|Φ0⟩​⟨Φf|(i​q​x)22|Φ0⟩∗\propto\langle\Phi_{f}|I|\Phi_{0}\rangle\langle\Phi_{f}|\frac{(iqx)^{2}}{2}|\Phi_{0}\rangle^{*} and its conjugate are zero from orthogonality. Thus, the sign of the term ∝q2\propto q^{2} in the anharmonic structure factor is strictly positive for producing an excited state, whereas there is no corresponding term ∝q2\propto q^{2} in the harmonic case for n≥2n\geq 2 phonons. Since we are probing the q≪2​md​ω0q\ll\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}} regime, this leading term quickly dominates the structure factor. Thus, the anharmonic scattering rate exceeds the harmonic rate in this regime. A consequence of this is that we expect the harmonic crystal result gives a lower bound on the scattering.

V Conclusions

Scattering of DM with nuclei in crystals necessarily goes through production of one or many phonons for DM masses smaller than ∼100\sim 100 MeV. Previous work has focused on calculating the multiphonon scattering rates in a harmonic crystal under the incoherent approximation (i.e. q>qBZq>q_{\mathrm{BZ}} or DM mass ≳\gtrsim MeV). In this work, we have studied the effects of anharmonicities in the crystal on the scattering rates, while still working within the incoherent approximation.

In order to obtain a tractable calculation of anharmonic effects, we have simplified the problem into a toy model of a single atom in a 1D anharmonic potential. In this toy model, scattering into multiphonons can still be well-approximated by applying a smearing on the spectrum of quantized states to account for the phonon spectrum of a lattice. We extract anharmonic couplings by modeling the interatomic potentials of Si and Ge, which give rise to realistic single atom potentials. This approach allows us to obtain an analytic understanding and first estimate of the impact of anharmonicity, although the numerical results should not be taken as a definitive rate calculation.

We find that the harmonic crystal results of Ref. [25] can be safely assumed for DM masses down to ∼10\sim 10 MeV. Below ∼10\sim 10 MeV, this assumption cannot be taken for granted. In this regime, we find that anharmonic effects on the scattering rates increase with decreasing DM mass and increasing experimental thresholds. Anharmonic corrections up to two orders of magnitude are possible for DM masses ∼\sim a few MeV and for experimental thresholds ∼\sim a few times the typical single phonon energy of the crystal. These findings are consistent with Refs. [37, 25], which studied two-phonon production from sub-MeV DM and found up to an order of magnitude larger rate from anharmonic couplings.

The size of the corrections is dependent on the material through the anharmonicity strength of that crystal and also, non-trivially, through the typical single phonon energies of the material. For a particular energy threshold, crystals with lower single phonon energies exhibit larger corrections since they require larger phonon numbers to be produced. For example, anharmonic effects in Ge can be larger by almost an order of magnitude than those in Si for similar DM parameter space and thresholds, even though the anharmonic couplings in the two crystals are similar. This is a consequence of the difference in qq scaling of the harmonic and anharmonic contributions, which become more pronounced with larger phonon number. Materials with low single-phonon energies, such as GaAs and Ge, therefore have the largest anharmonic effects. The effects will be reduced in Diamond and Al2O3, which have even higher single phonon energies than Si.

The relevance of anharmonic effects to direct detection experiments depends on the DM cross section. The effects are largest for low DM masses and high thresholds, in other words on the tails of the recoil spectrum where the rates are small. For a typical benchmark exposure of 1 kg-yr, the anharmonic corrections become sizeable for DM-nucleon cross sections above ∼10−34\sim 10^{-34} cm2. Being agnostic about any terrestrial or astrophysical constraints on the DM model and only requiring the DM to be observable in underground direct detection experiments, the upper bound on the DM cross section is σn≲10−28​cm2\sigma_{n}\lesssim 10^{-28}~\text{cm}^{2} [52]. This comes from considering an overburden of ∼\sim km. On the other hand, these very high DM-nucleon cross sections are typically excluded by terrestrial and astrophysical constraints for the simplest sub-GeV dark matter models [53, 54]. DM-nucleon cross sections σn≳10−41​cm2\sigma_{n}\gtrsim 10^{-41}~\text{cm}^{2} (σn≳10−31​cm2\sigma_{n}\gtrsim 10^{-31}~\text{cm}^{2}) are constrained for typical models with a heavy mediator (light dark photon mediator) for a DM mass ∼\sim MeV. With these constraints, we see from Fig. 10 that the anharmonic effects can only impart corrections of at most an order of magnitude for experiments with kg-yr exposure.

Experiments with exposures above kg-yr could see larger anharmonic effects, since they would be more sensitive to the events at high phonon number for MeV-scale DM. However, for solid-state direct detection experiments, achieving exposures significantly bigger than a kg-yr is challenging. Thus, for near-future crystal target experiments, we conclude that the anharmonic effects are only important up to 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) factors at masses of ∼\sim a few MeV for the simplest DM models.

Appendix A Interatomic potentials

In order to produce results for a real crystal, we adopt atomic potentials based on Ref. [49]. The interatomic potentials used here are a combination of various commonly used empirical potentials. We choose to use the Tersoff-Buckingham-Coulomb interatomic potential defined in Ref. [49] using the parameters in the set labeled “TBC-1”, though other interatomic potentials may be chosen and give similar estimates for the anharmonicity strengths.

This potential includes a three-body Tersoff potential, originally defined in [55], which we restate here for reference.

E\displaystyle E =12​∑i∑i≠jVi​j\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\sum_{i\neq j}V_{ij}
Vi​j\displaystyle V_{ij} =fC​(ri​j)​(fR​(ri​j)+bi​j​fA​(ri​j)),\displaystyle=f_{C}(r_{ij})\big(f_{R}(r_{ij})+b_{ij}f_{A}(r_{ij})\big), (80)

where the sum is over nearest-neighbor, and ri​jr_{ij} is the distance between neighbors i,ji,j. The function fCf_{C} is a cutoff function that keeps the interaction short ranged, fRf_{R} and fAf_{A} are repulsive and attractive interactions, and bi​jb_{ij} is a three-body term that is a function of the bonding angle of the third body with the atoms i,ji,j. Explicitly, these functions are defined as

fC​(r)={1r<R−D12−12​sin⁡(π2​r−RD)R−D<r<R+D0r>R+D\displaystyle f_{C}(r)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cll}1&\ \ r<R-D\\ \frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{r-R}{D}\right)&\ \ R-D<r<R+D\\ 0&\ \ r>R+D\end{array}\right.
fR​(r)=A​exp⁡(−λ1​r)\displaystyle f_{R}(r)=A\exp\left(-\lambda_{1}r\right) (84)
fA​(r)=−B​exp⁡(−λ2​r)\displaystyle f_{A}(r)=-B\exp\left(-\lambda_{2}r\right) (85)
bi​j=(1+βnζi​j)n−12​n\displaystyle b_{ij}=\left(1+\beta^{n}\zeta_{ij}{}^{n}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2n}} (86)
ζi​j=∑k≠i,jfC​(ri​k)​g​[θi​j​k​(ri​j,ri​k)]\displaystyle\zeta_{ij}=\sum_{k\neq i,j}f_{C}\left(r_{ik}\right)g\left[\theta_{ijk}\left(r_{ij},r_{ik}\right)\right]
×exp[λ3(ri​j−ri​k)mm]\displaystyle\qquad\quad\times\exp\left[\lambda_{3}{}^{m}\left(r_{ij}-r_{ik}\right)^{m}\right] (87)
g⁡(θ)=1+c2d2−c2[d2+(cos⁡θ−cos⁡θ0)2],\displaystyle g(\theta)=1+\frac{c^{2}}{d^{2}}-\frac{c^{2}}{\left[d^{2}+\left(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_{0}\right)^{2}\right]}, (88)

where θi​j​k\theta_{ijk} is the angle between the displacement vectors ri​jr_{ij} and ri​kr_{ik}. R,D,A,B,β,n,c,d,θ0,λ1,λ2,λ3R,D,A,B,\beta,n,c,d,\theta_{0},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3} are constants that can be found in Ref. [49]. Note that the notation in this section matches that of Ref. [49] and is standalone from the main text. Specifically, the parameters λ1,λ2,λ3\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3} are not to be confused with the anharmonicity strengths defined in the main text. In practice, anharmonicity arises from the asymmetry between the repulsive and attractive terms. The directional dependence of the anharmonicity strength is a result of the crystal’s zincblende structure and bond angle-dependent potential.

The other components of this interatomic model include a long-range two-body Buckingham term

V(r)=Ce−r/ρ−Er6,V(r)=Ce^{-r/\rho}-\frac{E}{r^{6}}, (89)

and a screened Coulombic interaction defined by

V⁡(r)\displaystyle V(r) =q2[erfc⁡(α​r)r−erfc⁡(α​rc)rc\displaystyle=q^{2}\Big[\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\alpha r)}{r}-\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\alpha r_{c})}{r_{c}}
+(erfc⁡(α​rc)rc2+2​απe−α2​rc2rc)(r−rc)]\displaystyle+\Big(\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\alpha r_{c})}{r_{c}^{2}}+\frac{2\alpha}{\sqrt{\pi}}\frac{e^{-\alpha^{2}r_{c}^{2}}}{r_{c}}\Big)(r-r_{c})\Big] (90)
×Θ⁡(rc−r)\displaystyle\times\Theta(r_{c}-r) (91)

Here qq is the effective atomic charge, α\alpha is a damping parameter, and rcr_{c} is a cutoff. As discussed in Ref. [49], the full interatomic potential model is a sum of the three aforementioned interactions. All of the free parameters are fit onto the actual second, third, and fourth order forces calculated from DFT. This gives an analytic interatomic potential that produces the correct single-phonon dispersions and also captures the anharmonicity in the potential by fitting onto the higher order interatomic forces from DFT.

Appendix B Power counting in perturbation theory

In this appendix, we work out the explicit relation between the powers of q2q^{2} and λk\lambda_{k} in the perturbation theory calculation for the anharmonic Hamiltonian in (36).

The primary object we focus on in the dynamic structure factor is the squared matrix element |⟨Φn|ei​q​x|Φ0⟩|2|\langle\Phi_{n}|e^{iqx}|\Phi_{0}\rangle|^{2}, where |Φn⟩|\Phi_{n}\rangle are the eigenstates of the anharmonic Hamiltonian. With perturbation theory, the eigenstates can be expanded in powers of λk\lambda_{k} as in (37). The corrections to the nnth final state up to second order in λk\lambda_{k} are given by,

|ψn(1)⟩\displaystyle|\psi_{n}^{(1)}\rangle =∑k≠nVk​n(n−k)​|k⟩,\displaystyle=\sum_{k\neq n}\frac{V_{kn}}{(n-k)}|k\rangle, (92)
|ψn(2)⟩\displaystyle|\psi_{n}^{(2)}\rangle =∑k≠n∑l≠nVk​l​Vl​n(n−k)​(n−l)​|k⟩−12​|n⟩​∑k≠n|Vk​n|2(n−k)2,\displaystyle=\sum_{k\neq n}\sum_{l\neq n}\frac{V_{kl}V_{ln}}{(n-k)(n-l)}|k\rangle-\frac{1}{2}|n\rangle\sum_{k\neq n}\frac{|V_{kn}|^{2}}{(n-k)^{2}},

where Vi​j≡⟨i|(2​md​ω0​x)k|j⟩V_{ij}\equiv\matrixelement{i}{(\sqrt{2m_d\omega_0}x)^k}{j}. In terms of the standard ladder operators of the harmonic oscillator, Vi​jV_{ij} are given by,

Vi​j=⟨i|(a+a†)k|j⟩.\displaystyle V_{ij}=\matrixelement{i}{(a+a^{\dagger})^k}{j}. (93)

This tells us that Vi​jV_{ij} can only be non-zero when i−ji-j is one of the following: −k-k, −k+2-k+2,…, k−2k-2, kk.

With these selection rules, the corrections in Eqs. 92 can be schematically written as,

+|n+k−2⟩+|n+k⟩\displaystyle\quad+|n+k-2\rangle+|n+k\rangle (94)

+λk{(q22​md​ω0)n−k/2+(q22​md​ω0)n−k/2+1\displaystyle\qquad+\lambda_{k}\Big\{\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{n-k/2}+\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{n-k/2+1}
+…+(q22​md​ω0)n+k/2}\displaystyle\qquad\quad+...+\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{n+k/2}\Big\}
+λk2{(q22​md​ω0)n−k+(q22​md​ω0)n−k+1\displaystyle\qquad+\lambda_{k}^{2}\Big\{\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{n-k}+\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{n-k+1}
+…+(q22​md​ω0)n+k}+𝒪(λk3)].\displaystyle\qquad\quad+...+\Big(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}\Big)^{n+k}\Big\}+\mathcal{O}(\lambda_{k}^{3})\Big]. (110)

Thus we see that we get corrections at all orders in λk\lambda_{k}, with the lowest non-zero power being λk\lambda_{k}. In general, at 𝒪⁡(λkj)\mathcal{O}(\lambda_{k}^{j}), the lowest power of q2q^{2} is n−(j×k)/2n-(j\times k)/2, and the highest power is n+(j×k)/2n+(j\times k)/2. Following similar arguments to the case of odd kk discussed earlier, ν⁡(n,i)\nu(n,i) for i>1i>1 is given by,

ν⁡(n,i)=max​(⌈|n−i|k/2⌉,1).\displaystyle\nu(n,i)=\text{max}\Big(\lceil\frac{|n-i|}{k/2}\rceil~,~1\Big). (111)

Another difference between the case of even kk considered here and that of odd kk is that we do not get an i=1i=1 term for even nn, as all terms in the coefficients bjb_{j} contain even powers of qq. This means that the leading term will always go as q4q^{4}, with a λk\lambda_{k} power determined by (111) for i=2i=2. For odd nn, the lowest power of qq in bjb_{j} is n−k×jn-k\times j. Thus, in the squared matrix element, the lowest non-zero power ν⁡(n,1)\nu(n,1) required is given by,

ν⁡(n,1)=max​(2×⌈|n−1|k⌉,1).\displaystyle\nu(n,1)=\text{max}\Big(2\times\lceil\frac{|n-1|}{k}\rceil~,~1\Big). (112)

The calculations in this appendix up to this point consider the overall scaling behavior of the powers of q2q^{2} and λk\lambda_{k} in the squared matrix element. We have neglected combinatorial factors at several steps in the calculations that enter into the numerical coefficients an,ia_{n,i} in (102). Sometimes, the numerical coefficients can also cancel with each other, and the naive leading behavior estimated in this section can vanish. In order to give concrete examples of the numerical coefficients, we perform explicit calculations of the squared matrix element using perturbation theory with k=3k=3 (i.e. a cubic perturbation), and phonon numbers n=1,2,3,and​4n=1,~2,~3,~\text{and}~4. We perform this explicit calculation only up to 𝒪⁡(λ32)\mathcal{O}(\lambda_{3}^{2}). The results of various numerical coefficients are presented below.

For a single-phonon production (i.e. n=1n=1), the coefficients an,ia_{n,i} are given by,

a1,1\displaystyle a_{1,1} =44\displaystyle=44 (113)
a1,2\displaystyle a_{1,2} =−82\displaystyle=-82 (114)
a1,3\displaystyle a_{1,3} =5.\displaystyle=5. (115)

For a two-phonon production (i.e. n=2n=2), the coefficients are given by,

a2,1\displaystyle a_{2,1} =8\displaystyle=8 (116)
a2,2\displaystyle a_{2,2} =59\displaystyle=59 (117)
a2,3\displaystyle a_{2,3} =−56\displaystyle=-56 (118)
a2,4\displaystyle a_{2,4} =2.5.\displaystyle=2.5. (119)

For a three-phonon production (i.e. n=3n=3), the coefficients are,

a3,2\displaystyle a_{3,2} =18\displaystyle=18 (120)
a3,3\displaystyle a_{3,3} =37\displaystyle=37 (121)
a3,4\displaystyle a_{3,4} =−23.04\displaystyle=-23.04 (122)
a3,5\displaystyle a_{3,5} =0.77.\displaystyle=0.77. (123)

Note that we do not show the coefficient a3,1a_{3,1} as it appears at 𝒪⁡(λ34)\mathcal{O}(\lambda_{3}^{4}). Finally, for a four-phonon production (i.e. n=4n=4), the coefficients are evaluated to be,

a4,1\displaystyle a_{4,1} =0\displaystyle=0 (124)
a4,2\displaystyle a_{4,2} =0\displaystyle=0 (125)
a4,3\displaystyle a_{4,3} =0.097\displaystyle=0.097 (126)
a4,4\displaystyle a_{4,4} =0.05\displaystyle=0.05 (127)
a4,5\displaystyle a_{4,5} =−0.012\displaystyle=-0.012 (128)
a4,6\displaystyle a_{4,6} =1.81×10−4.\displaystyle=1.81\times 10^{-4}. (129)

Note that the coefficients a4,1a_{4,1} and a4,2a_{4,2} amount to zero because of a numerical cancellation between the two terms in the b1b_{1} coefficient in Eq. 98. The leading behavior of the terms proportional to q2q^{2} and q4q^{4} in the structure factor is instead q2​λ36q^{2}\lambda_{3}^{6} and q4​λ34q^{4}\lambda_{3}^{4}, respectively.

As these numerical coefficients appear through combinations and interferences of several combinatorial factors at various steps of the calculation, it is hard to provide a general expression for them. By looking at the examples above however, we can make some general observations. Typically, we see that the coefficients follow a pyramid structure, with an,ia_{n,i} being the largest for ii near nn, and decreasing with ii away from nn. We also find that the coefficients can vary by orders of magnitude from each other. The terms with ii near nn receive contributions from several individual matrix elements, and in general seem to be larger. We expect to see this pattern continue for higher phonon numbers as well. The exact values of these coefficients play a role in determining where the anharmonic corrections dominate, and so our power counting approach only gives an O⁡(1)O(1) estimate.

Appendix C Impulse approximation

In Sec. III.3, we calculated the structure factor via the saddle point approximation in the regime defined by (52). This regime corresponded to values of ω\omega near q22​m\frac{q^{2}}{2m} and within the Gaussian width of (63). As discussed in the main text, in order to calculate the tail of the structure factor far from ω=q22​m,\omega=\frac{q^{2}}{2m}, more expansion terms are needed in ff. Here we discuss this extension of the impulse approximation.

First, in the special case of a harmonic potential, we can start from the full result in Eq. (35). After rewriting the energy conservation delta function as a time integral, we find that

f⁡(t)=−i​ω​t+q22​md​ω0​(ei​ω0​t−1)f(t)=-i\omega t+\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega_{0}}(e^{i\omega_{0}t}-1) (130)

Solving f′​(t)=0f^{\prime}(t)=0 gives the exact result

tI=iω0​ln⁡(q22​md​ω).t_{I}=\frac{i}{\omega_{0}}\ln\left(\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{d}\omega}\right). (131)

Using the saddle point approximation for ω≫ω0\omega\gg\omega_{0}, we find

Stoy,d​(q,ω)∼1ω​ω0​e−2​Wtoy​(q)​(q22​m​ω)ωω0​eωω0.S_{\textrm{toy},d}(q,\omega)\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{\omega\omega_{0}}}\,e^{-2W_{\rm toy}(q)}\left(\frac{q^{2}}{2m{\omega}}\right)^{\frac{\omega}{\omega_{0}}}e^{\frac{\omega}{\omega_{0}}}. (132)

The same result can also be derived by approximating the sum over phonon states as an integral in Eq. (35). The saddle point approximation for the harmonic oscillator holds as long as ω≫ω0\omega\gg\omega_{0}, and we no longer have a condition on how close ω\omega is to q22​m\frac{q^{2}}{2m}. In the impulse regime, ω∼q22​m\omega\sim\frac{q^{2}}{2m}, one can check that it reduces to the previous result in Eq. (63). We see in this exact result that the tail at large ω\omega is Poissonian instead of Gaussian.

For general potentials, this exact analytic result is no longer possible, but we can still calculate corrections to the tail. First, we start by giving the exact saddle point equation:

0=f′​(tI)=−i⁡(E0+ω−q22​m)+i​⟨H′​ei​H′​tI⟩⟨ei​H′​tI⟩0=f^{\prime}(t_{I})=-i\left(E_{0}+\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m}\right)+i\frac{\left\langle H^{\prime}e^{iH^{\prime}t_{I}}\right\rangle}{\left\langle e^{iH^{\prime}t_{I}}\right\rangle} (133)

which is valid at all orders. We begin by noticing that saddle point equation (133) is satisfied exactly at ω=q22​m\omega=\frac{q^{2}}{2m} by tI=0t_{I}=0. Then, ω\omega-derivatives of tIt_{I} at ω=q22​m\omega=\frac{q^{2}}{2m} can be found by taking ω\omega-derivatives of (133) and solving for tI(n)[ω=q22​m]t_{I}^{(n)}[\omega=\frac{q^{2}}{2m}]. This allows us to calculate tI[ω=q22​m]t_{I}[\omega=\frac{q^{2}}{2m}] in an iterative fashion. The first few terms are

tI​[q22​m]\displaystyle t_{I}[\frac{q^{2}}{2m}] =0\displaystyle=0
tI′​[q22​m]\displaystyle t_{I}^{\prime}[\frac{q^{2}}{2m}] =i⟨H′⟩2−⟨H′2⟩\displaystyle=\frac{i}{\langle H^{\prime}\rangle^{2}-\langle H^{\prime 2}\rangle}

where tI(n)t_{I}^{(n)} denotes the nnth ω\omega-derivative of tIt_{I}. In the harmonic case, this series resums to (131). For general potentials, one can then use the expansions (60) and (134) to calculate

Stoy,d​(q,ω)≈2​π−f′′​(tI)​ef⁡(tI)S_{\text{toy},d}(q,\omega)\approx\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{-f^{\prime\prime}(t_{I})}}e^{f(t_{I})} (135)

to a desired order.

Appendix D Exact results for Morse potential

The Morse potential is a special case of an anharmonic potential where the structure factor is analytically solvable. We will use this case to illustrate the behavior of the structure factor discussed in Sec. III.2. We also use it to validate the numerical calculations used in our final results and check the validity of the impulse approximation in the regime where there are n>10n>10 phonons.

The Morse potential is defined as

VMorse=B⁡(e−2​a​x−2​e−a​x),V_{\mathrm{Morse}}=B\Big(e^{-2ax}-2e^{-ax}\Big), (136)

where aa is a parameter controlling the width of the potential and BB is the normalization. Expanding this potential in powers of xx gives

VMorse=−B+B​a2​x2−B​a3​x3+712​B​a4​x4+…\displaystyle V_{\mathrm{Morse}}=-B+Ba^{2}x^{2}-Ba^{3}x^{3}+\frac{7}{12}Ba^{4}x^{4}+... (137)

Matching the quadratic and the cubic terms with (26), we find that

a\displaystyle a =−4​λ3​2​m​ω0\displaystyle=-4\lambda_{3}\sqrt{2m\omega_{0}} (138)
B\displaystyle B =ω064​λ32.\displaystyle=\frac{\omega_{0}}{64\lambda_{3}^{2}}. (139)

Note that the Morse potential has fewer free parameters than the anharmonic potential up to fourth order in the displacements, so we cannot simultaneously fit λ4\lambda_{4}. Nonetheless, the realistic potential as obtained App. A are well approximated by this Morse potential due to the dominance and Morse-like behavior of the fRf_{R} and fAf_{A} terms in the Tersoff part of the potential.

The Morse potential approximation of our anharmonic potential is then given by

VMorse=ω064​λM2​(e8​λM​2​m​ω0−2​e4​λM​2​m​ω0​x),V_{\mathrm{Morse}}=\frac{\omega_{0}}{64\lambda_{M}^{2}}\Big(e^{8\lambda_{M}\sqrt{2m\omega_{0}}}-2e^{4\lambda_{M}\sqrt{2m\omega_{0}}x}\Big), (140)

where we take λM=λ3\lambda_{M}=\lambda_{3} in order to fit up to third order anharmonicities. In this potential, the structure factor (68) is exactly calculable since the Morse eigenstates and eigenenergies are known analytically. These results [56] give squared matrix elements between the ground state and nnth excited state of

|⟨Φn|ei​q​x|Φ0⟩|2=(2​K−2​n−1)​(2​K−1)n!​Γ​(2​K)​Γ​(2​K−n)\displaystyle|\langle\Phi_{n}|e^{iqx}|\Phi_{0}\rangle|^{2}=\frac{(2K-2n-1)(2K-1)}{n!\Gamma(2K)\Gamma(2K-n)}
×|Γ⁡(n+i⁡(q/2​m​ω0)4​λM)​Γ​(2​K+i⁡(q/2​m​ω0)4​λM−n−1)Γ⁡(i​q/2​m​ω04​λM)|2,\displaystyle\times\absolutevalue{\frac{\Gamma(n + \frac{i(q/\sqrt{2m \omega_0})}{4\lambda_M}) \Gamma(2K + \frac{i(q/\sqrt{2m \omega_0})}{4\lambda_M} - n - 1)}{\Gamma(\frac{iq/\sqrt{2m \omega_0}}{4\lambda_M})}}^{2}, (141)

with energy gaps

En−E0=(n−n⁡(1+n)2​K)​ω0,E_{n}-E_{0}=\big(n-\frac{n(1+n)}{2K}\Big)\omega_{0}, (142)

where K=132​λM2K=\frac{1}{32\lambda_{M}^{2}}.

Note that these formulae are only valid for n<K−12n<K-\frac{1}{2} since above this excited state, the eigenstates are unbound and have a different analytic form. For λM∼0.01\lambda_{M}\sim 0.01, this condition requires n≲312n\lesssim 312, which corresponds to an energy gap of 𝒪⁡(eV)\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{eV}). Recoil energies at this scale are comparable to the size of a typical lattice potential well and thus the free nuclear recoil approximation holds. Then, for typical anharmonicity strengths, the discrete states of the Morse potential that we have used in this analysis are sufficient to estimate the anharmonic effect in the multiphonon scattering regime.

Putting together expressions (141)-(148), (68), and (72) we can calculate the structure factor in the Morse potential in both the large and small qq regime. We show these results for λM=λ3\lambda_{M}=\lambda_{3} in Figs. 11 and 12. Fig. 11 provides a check for our numerical results in Sec. IV. Here we see that the numerical calculations and corresponding analytic Morse results are almost identical. There is a modified qq scaling of the structure factor compared to the harmonic case, as was already illustrated in Fig. 7. We can also obtain this behavior analytically with the Morse potential. Expanding the expression (141) to leading order in qq and subsequently in λM\lambda_{M}, we get explicitly,

|⟨2|ei​q​x|0⟩|2\displaystyle|\langle 2|e^{iqx}|0\rangle|^{2} =8​λM2​q2+…\displaystyle=8\lambda_{M}^{2}q^{2}+\ldots (143)
|⟨3|ei​q​x|0⟩|2\displaystyle|\langle 3|e^{iqx}|0\rangle|^{2} =5123​λM4​q2+…\displaystyle=\frac{512}{3}\lambda_{M}^{4}q^{2}+\ldots (144)
|⟨4|ei​q​x|0⟩|2\displaystyle|\langle 4|e^{iqx}|0\rangle|^{2} =6144​λM6​q2+…,\displaystyle=6144\lambda_{M}^{6}q^{2}+\ldots, (145)
|⟨5|ei​q​x|0⟩|2\displaystyle|\langle 5|e^{iqx}|0\rangle|^{2} =15728645​λM8​q2+…,\displaystyle=\frac{1572864}{5}\lambda_{M}^{8}q^{2}+\ldots, (146)
|⟨6|ei​q​x|0⟩|2\displaystyle|\langle 6|e^{iqx}|0\rangle|^{2} =20971520​λM10​q2+…,\displaystyle=20971520\lambda_{M}^{10}q^{2}+\ldots, (147)

where the ellipses include higher orders in both qq and λM\lambda_{M}. The leading λM\lambda_{M} scalings are consistent with those illustrated in Fig. 4 for n=2n=2 and 33. For n=4n=4, the leading λM\lambda_{M} scaling differs from the power counting in Fig. 4, but matches with the explicit results obtained using perturbation theory as presented in Appendix B. An exact numerical cancellation modifies the leading behavior to λM6​q2\lambda_{M}^{6}q^{2}. We see that the leading behavior in q,λMq,\lambda_{M} for n>4n>4 also differs from the x3x^{3}-theory power counting, suggesting a generic presence of cancellations at lower orders of λ3\lambda_{3} for the q2q^{2} dependence.

In Fig. 12, we demonstrate that the impulse approximation remains robust for q≫2​md​ω0q\gg\sqrt{2m_{d}\omega_{0}} and n>10n>10 excited states. Note that we can also calculate corrections to ⟨p2⟩\langle p^{2}\rangle in the Morse ground state exactly:

⟨p2⟩=m​ω02​(1−16​λM2),\langle p^{2}\rangle=\frac{m\omega_{0}}{2}(1-16\lambda_{M}^{2}), (148)

which is used in the impulse regime result (63). The impulse result is almost identical between the Morse and harmonic cases, since the Gaussian width is only corrected at order λM2,\lambda_{M}^{2}, which is ∼10−4.\sim 10^{-4}. This is also borne out in the full calculation of the structure factor shown in Fig. 12.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
